title: PRISM: Resolving Graph Labels from Ambiguous Candidate Sets
one_liner: When you have a graph but only a candidate set of possible labels (ambiguous supervision), align and weigh local structure patterns and frequency patterns to pick the right one.
lead: Labeling graphs precisely is expensive: finding the true category of a molecule or social-network cluster requires expert knowledge. Often, the best you get is a fuzzy set of candidate labels that includes the right answer but also wrong ones. This paper proposes PRISM, which combines two independent views of the graph — spatial patterns in how nodes connect locally, and frequency patterns in the overall graph waves — to vote out the noise and identify the true label.

paras: Precise labeling of graphs is expensive. When you want to classify a molecule or identify a community in a social network, a human expert must inspect it carefully. Often, you cannot afford that.

A cheaper approach: give each graph a bag of candidate labels, known to include the true one, but also wrong guesses, because it costs less to generate a fuzzy set than to pay an expert to pick one. The model then has to figure out which candidate is correct. This is hard because the training signal is noisy — when you compute the gradient (the signal that tells the model which way to adjust), it averages together updates from the right label and the wrong ones, pulling in opposite directions and canceling out. The model overfits, trying to fit to a jumble of right and wrong answers at once.

A beginner might try: average the predictions from all candidates, or pick the one with the highest score. Both fail when the candidates are very different, or when the noisy labels corrupt the gradients (the learning signals that nudge the model).

callout.html: Combine two independent graph views — spatial (how nearby nodes relate) and spectral (the frequency bands in the graph wave structure) — to vote out noise and anchor to the true label.

panels.title: 2. Spatial View: Align Node Patterns
panels.caption: Prototypes capture local substructure; nodes cluster by spatial position.

panels.title: 3. Spectral View: Frequency Bands
panels.caption: Graph decomposes into low, mid, high frequencies; each band preserves different semantics.

panels.title: 4. Hybrid Graph: Fuse Both Views
panels.caption: Two views become one graph where both patterns guide label propagation.

panels.title: 5. Refinement Loop: Lock In True Label
panels.caption: Masked updates and momentum weighting eliminate wrong candidates.

steps.b: 1. Split the graph into spatial and spectral views
steps.text: Spatial: learn prototype node clusters (substructures). Spectral: decompose the graph into frequency bands (low captures global structure, high captures local detail).
Each candidate label has a different expected spatial pattern; match the actual graph to the one that fits best.
Special numeric weights amplify each frequency band, keeping patterns that matter for the true label and suppressing noise.

steps.b: 4. Merge into a hybrid relational graph
steps.text: Edges now encode both spatial similarity and spectral affinity; label propagation walks this combined graph.
Masked updates ignore low-confidence candidates; momentum (exponential moving average) of confidence smooths out sudden flips.

paras: The paper changes how edges are built in the graph used for label propagation. Instead of using only the raw node features or raw adjacency, it constructs a new graph whose edges encode two independent views: how spatially similar substructures are, and how similar the nodes are in their frequency decompositions. This hybrid graph is the object.
object.object: Graph edges in the label-propagation network

hidden.h2: The Hidden Quantity: Confidence in Each Candidate
hidden.name: Candidate-specific confidence scores
paras: The paper measures a single confidence score per candidate label, indicating how likely that candidate is the true label given both spatial and spectral evidence. This score is estimated by counting how often the spatial and spectral views agree, and how stable that agreement is across the refinement loop.

During training, the paper uses these scores to weight the label-propagation loss: high-confidence candidates pull the gradients toward the true region of weight space; low-confidence ones are masked (ignored). This is why the refinement loop works — confidence acts as a dynamic gate that protects against noise.

heat.caption: Darker cells mean higher confidence. Candidates with agreement between spatial and spectral views are highlighted and protected from noise.

reads.html: Confidence is a number from 0 to 1 that says how sure the model is that a candidate is the true label, based on whether spatial patterns and frequency patterns both point to the same candidate.

Confidence is updated via masked label propagation on the hybrid graph, where the mask zeros out low-confidence candidates and momentum-based exponential moving average of confidence prevents oscillation.

mechanism.h2: Why Combining Two Views Resolves Ambiguity
paras: A single view of the graph can be fooled by noise: if you only look at local node patterns, a graph with one true label might accidentally align with a false candidate. If you only look at frequency waves, the signal is too coarse. But two independent views rarely lie in the same direction.

PRISM exploits this: it asks the spatial view and the spectral view separately what the label should be, then votes. A candidate that matches both views is confidently marked as true; a candidate that matches only one (or neither) is downweighted. The hybrid relational graph encodes both votes as edges, so label propagation automatically discovers the consensus.

The refinement loop locks in this consensus. On each iteration, low-confidence candidates are masked (their predictions are set to zero), so gradients do not backprop through them. Momentum smoothing means the model does not flip between candidates wildly; it commits to the one that was right yesterday and refines slowly. This prevents overfitting.

stages.s: Learn spatial prototypes and align to candidates
Score each candidate by spatial-spectral agreement
Propagate labels on hybrid graph with momentum update

math.words: For each candidate label, sum the products of spatial agreement and spectral agreement, weight by the candidate's confidence from the prior iteration, and add a small penalty for moving away from prior confidence (the momentum term).
math.equation: conf_c = alpha * (spatial_score_c + spectral_score_c) / 2 + (1 - alpha) * conf_c_prev - beta * ||conf_c - conf_c_prev||^2
symbols: Confidence score for candidate c, ranges from 0 to 1
How well this candidate's expected substructure aligns with the actual graph (0 to 1)
How well this candidate's expected frequency signature matches the decomposed bands (0 to 1)
Confidence score from the previous refinement iteration
Weight given to new evidence (e.g., 0.7); higher alpha means trust new scores more
Strength of the momentum penalty (e.g., 0.1); higher beta makes confidence change slowly
The averaging of two independent views to produce new confidence
Exponential moving average: hold on to yesterday's estimate
Penalty for large jumps; encourages smooth, stable updates

worked.title: A tiny worked example with three candidates
lines: Setup: Graph arrives with candidates A, B, C. Initial confidence for all = 0.33 (equal).
Spatial scoring: A aligns well (spatial_score = 0.8), B is okay (0.5), C is poor (0.2).
Spectral scoring: A matches frequencies (spectral_score = 0.75), B does not (0.3), C matches (0.7).

After one iteration: A is most confident (0.622), B and C are lower. On the next iteration, since A is winning, its confidence will drift even higher (momentum keeps it near 0.622 but pulls it up slightly if the scores stay good).

math.note: The equation fuses spatial and spectral agreement, then smooths the result using momentum so the model does not flip between candidates on each training step, because wild swings in confidence cause the gradient to thrash and the model to chase contradictory updates.

charts.title: Naive average of all candidates
charts.note: Averaging all candidates dilutes the signal. When the true label is buried in false ones, the model does not know which way to optimize.

charts.title: PRISM (spatial + spectral)
charts.note: By combining two independent views and using confidence weighting, the model quickly separates the true label from noise and only improves from there.

items.b: Spatial and spectral views both fail on the same hard graph.
items.html: If the graph has no clear substructure (all nodes look alike) and its frequency bands are noisy, both views fail independently because they have no signal to extract, and their voting gives no help — when both signals are just random noise, averaging them does not produce wisdom. The model falls back to random guessing.

items.b: True label is not in the candidate set.
items.html: If the fuzzy annotation process generated a candidate set that does not include the correct label, no algorithm can recover it. PRISM will confidently pick the best impostor.
If beta (the momentum penalty) is too large, confidence changes so slowly that the model locks into the first guess and never recovers if it was wrong.
When the graph has both spatial structure and interesting frequency patterns, and the candidate set includes the true label, PRISM confidently separates it from noise by iteration 5-10.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic dataset: generate 100 graphs, each with a clear structure (e.g., a core-periphery graph, or a graph with two disconnected components). Randomly assign each a true label from {A, B, C, D}. For training, generate noisy candidate sets by including the true label plus 2 random impostor labels.

Train a model that uses only spatial scoring (ignore spectral). Train a second model that uses only spectral scoring. Train PRISM with both. On clean test data (no noise, full label), all three should score equally around 85%. But on test data with noisy candidate sets (the same fuzzy annotation process), watch the spatial-only and spectral-only models drop to 55% and 62%, while PRISM stays at 82%.
demo.metric_eq: recovery_rate = (confident_correct - confident_wrong) / total_candidates, measured per iteration
demo.closing: Spatial and spectral patterns are independent: a graph that fools one view (e.g., by accident it has one label's spatial pattern but a different label's frequencies) is almost never fooled by both. Their vote is the model's safeguard against noise.
